title: Autistic Experience at School: Communication, Connection and Identity

segments.spoken_text:
Welcome back. We’re moving now from our shared understanding of autism into the experience of a school day. You’ll find the Session Three summary on page ten of your Participant Guide. Bring back the two or three students you’ve been holding in mind. Keep them as different people, with different strengths, preferences and experiences.
We’ll begin with communication and connection, then look at capacity: what a day asks of each student, what helps and what may accumulate over time. You’ll map a school day, and then turn to your own position as an early career teacher: finding out when you don’t have the answers, and knowing who to go to.
If you don’t have your own class yet, use a placement class or a class you know well. If you teach secondary, think across subjects, rooms and teachers as well as within your own lesson. A relief teacher can use a recent booking or a class they return to often.
The timetable tells us where students are meant to be and what happens next. It doesn’t tell us everything about how the day feels or what it takes to participate. Keep examples within education practice, leave out identifying details, and stay curious about what we don’t yet know. Your day map and support map will travel into the design work after lunch.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s begin with communication. Speech is one way of communicating, and we’ll be looking at a much wider picture: how students receive information, how they share what matters to them, and the ways we make both possible.
The amount someone speaks doesn’t tell us how much they understand. A student may need different ways to understand an instruction, answer a question, ask for help, request a pause or say no. All of those messages matter. Communication access belongs in the design of the classroom and the school day.
We’ll talk about practical options, including augmentative and alternative communication, or A A C. There isn’t one approach that suits every student. Individual assessment and intervention questions belong with the student’s speech pathologist or relevant team; our focus here is what educators can notice, make available and change.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s start with a quick, quiet think. Since you woke up this morning, how have you communicated? See if you can think of three different ways. Perhaps you spoke, sent a message, pointed, showed someone a photo, moved away, or took a moment before answering.
Give yourself about twenty seconds. Then, if you’re with colleagues, two or three people might share one example. Sharing is optional. Pause the video now if you’d like that thinking and sharing time.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s come back together. We move between ways of communicating all day, often without noticing. Writing, facial expression, gesture, sign, a communication device and speech are all real communication. One method isn’t more valid because it is spoken.
That gives us something useful to notice at school. When we say, ‘Use your words,’ are we overlooking a message a student has already communicated? A point, a look, or moving closer or further away can be worth attending to. Our job is to listen across the ways that person communicates, while checking what a message means rather than assuming.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 3: How did you communicate today?. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. segments.spoken_text:
There are two parts to keep distinct here: understanding and expressing. Understanding is information coming in and making sense. That might be a spoken instruction, a written sequence, a demonstration, or a gesture in context. Expressing is a message going out: an idea, a feeling, a question or a choice, through any communication method.
At school, a primary student may receive much of this information from one teacher, while a secondary student may receive it from several teachers across the day. The forms and expectations can change between lessons.
These don’t necessarily look the same for one person. Someone may speak at length and still need support to understand spoken information. Someone else may understand much more than they can readily express. Neither fluent speech nor limited speech gives us the whole picture. Communication can also change with the person, the place, the demands and how someone is feeling.
A A C means augmentative and alternative communication. It can include gesture, signs, a communication board or book, typing, or a communication device. Some people use it alongside speech and some instead of speech.
Repeated or scripted words can carry meaning too. Listen for the context and possible purpose before correcting the form. We don’t need to assign a language-processing label before respecting a student’s communication. If we need an individual assessment, we involve the relevant team. For our classroom practice, the question is: what does this environment help the student understand, and what ways does it give them to respond?

segments.spoken_text: We’re going to hear Autistic people describe communication in their own words. As you watch, notice what supports communication. Choose one idea that stands out to you. Let the speakers’ experiences lead your thinking, without expecting one account to describe every Autistic person.

segments.spoken_text: What stood out to you about what supported communication? Take a moment to choose one idea. You might think about a communication strength, something another person did that helped, or the difference the environment or available communication method made. If you’re watching with colleagues, invite one or two brief responses. Pause here for that conversation.

segments.spoken_text:
As we come back, hold onto that specific idea. There is no single Autistic communication profile, so we need to listen to what helps the particular person.
One practical point to carry into school is availability. A student’s communication system needs to be where communication happens: in class, at break, during transitions and when plans change. It cannot be limited to one activity or a therapy session. We support the student’s ways of communicating, working with the student, their family and the relevant team. We aren’t prescribing a system from a workshop example.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to page eleven of your Participant Guide, or use a sheet of paper. Put one of the students you have in mind in the centre. Around them are home, school, friends, community and supports. Who is part of this student’s communication network?
Add just one person or place now. Use roles rather than names: a family member, a classmate, a teacher, someone at a club. You can write, draw or use dot points. If it helps, ask a colleague to scribe your ideas.
You don’t need to fill every space. Networks can be small or changing, and an empty box is fine. Give yourself about a minute and a half. Pause the video while you make that first addition.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.

segments.spoken_text:
Keep that map open. You can return to the rest later. Different people and places may reveal different parts of a student’s communication. A family member, a classroom teacher and a support worker may each notice something valuable.
We’re not deciding who understands the student best. We’re recognising that the picture is shared. Where we know little about part of that network, we have a question to explore with the student and family, rather than a gap to fill with an assumption.

segments.spoken_text:
Now let’s think about what should travel between those people and places, so the student doesn’t have to start again with every new person. We’ll use three colours. Purple is a communication strength. Blue is something that helps communication. Orange is something you would like others to know.
Write one note, two, or all three. You can use one of your students, without identifying them, or a made-up example. If you don’t have coloured notes, label the three categories on paper. This is also on page eleven.
Allow about three minutes to write. Then, if you’re together, spend a few minutes sharing. You can add a note to the board or read one out, and you can keep your notes private. Leave any note with identifying details off the shared board. Pause now for the writing and optional sharing.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s bring our attention back. Look across the ideas available to you. What similarities do you notice? What strengths might be missed if we looked only for speech? Which supports involve changing what other people do or provide?
Think about what would help a relief teacher, a specialist or subject teacher, or staff on duty at break times. Useful knowledge can travel between classrooms, subjects, break times and home, with the student’s and family’s perspectives included. It can make continuity possible when the people around a student change.
Keep the blue notes in view: the things that help communication. We’re going to connect those ideas with three practical options.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 7: What should travel between people and places?. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 7; supplied slide, speaker notes and matching facilitator guide. Adapted/reused spoken delivery checked against this audience and the current Participant Guide. Primary source segment: s03_sl07_return. Session 3, active slide 7; slide text, speaker notes and corresponding facilitator guide.

segments.spoken_text:
The first option is clear communication. Use familiar, specific words and give one idea or step at a time, in a form and amount the person can access. That might mean making a direction shorter or making the first step clearer.
The second is processing time. After giving information, pause. A person may be making sense of what you said, organising a response and communicating it. If we fill every pause with a new version of the question, we may add more information before the earlier information has been processed.
The third is visual support: showing information as well as saying it, so there is something to return to.
These are options to match to the person and the moment, rather than a checklist that guarantees success. Keep the student’s A A C available and accept their preferred ways of responding, including refusal. A useful communication support makes messages easier to understand and share. It doesn’t require the student to produce the answer or communication style we were expecting.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 8: How can we support communication? 1. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 8; supplied slide, speaker notes and matching facilitator guide. Adapted/reused spoken delivery checked against this audience and the current Participant Guide. Primary source segment: s03_sl08_a. Session 3, active slide 8; slide text, speaker notes and corresponding facilitator guide.

segments.spoken_text:
Visual supports are information you can see and come back to. The three examples here answer different questions. A timer can show how much time is left. A sequence can show what to do next. A daily schedule can show what is happening today. You may already use a calendar, a shopping list or a reminder on your phone in much the same way.
The format needs to make sense to the person. Objects, photographs, written words and symbols can all be options, on paper or on a device. Check that the student understands what the information represents and can reach it when it is needed. A support displayed across the room may exist without being useful at the moment of need.
Think of the visual information already available in your classroom, or something you have seen on placement. What question does it answer? Could a student return to it without asking an adult? A visual support offers information; it isn’t a condition the student must satisfy to access something they enjoy.
Visual supports and A A C can overlap, but they aren’t interchangeable. Keep the person’s communication methods available as well. We’ll return to this in Session Four when you choose options for your day-one classroom setup.

segments.spoken_text:
Double empathy asks us to look at understanding in both directions. When people have different experiences and ways of communicating, it can be harder for them to understand one another. That doesn’t mean every social misunderstanding sits inside the Autistic student.
Consider a classroom discussion, group task or playground interaction. Whose expectations are shaping what counts as joining in? Who is expected to adjust? What would make this interaction clearer or safer for the people involved?
For example, an adult might expect a quick spoken response as a sign of connection. A student might connect through a shared activity, through detailed talk about an interest, or with more time between turns. Those are possible differences to explore, not conclusions to impose on a particular child.
The question is how each student connects. Connection doesn’t need to look one way. Our expectations and the context shape the interaction too, so we have something useful to examine and change. We can make room for different ways of being together while continuing to listen to what each person actually wants.

segments.spoken_text: Let’s carry that idea into the many ways students connect. As we watch this next clip, keep the question open: how does each student connect? Notice people, places, activities and ways of joining. A different style of connection is not evidence that connection is absent.

segments.spoken_text: Keep those possibilities in mind as we widen the picture beyond a single interaction. We can look for connection in a student’s preferred activities and relationships, while allowing their own ways of showing it to guide us.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 11: Being social. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 11; supplied slide, speaker notes and matching facilitator guide. Session 3, active slide 11; slide text, speaker notes and corresponding facilitator guide.

segments.spoken_text:
A student’s social world can include family, school, community and online spaces. Connection might be one to one, playing or working alongside someone, sharing a great deal about an interest, or seeing someone only occasionally. Being together quietly can matter as much as a lively conversation.
Culture also shapes expectations about interaction and relationships. We need to be careful about treating the pattern most familiar to us as the measure of meaningful connection for everyone.
There may be spaces outside home and school where a student feels a particular sense of belonging: a club, a community activity, or another shared-interest space. There may be online connections too. We don’t need to disclose a student’s online activity, identity or community membership to recognise that these possibilities exist.
Keep the picture individual. What do we know about this student’s preferred people, places and ways of joining? What are we assuming? What could we find out respectfully?

segments.spoken_text:
Find a partner for a conversation about connection. The questions are on page twelve of your Participant Guide. First, when do the students you have in mind seem most comfortable connecting with others at school? Second, what kinds of connection does each enjoy? That might be talking, gaming, sport, making things, shared interests, or being together quietly.
Third, are there times when being social seems enjoyable, and times when it seems tiring or overwhelming? Finally, what could educators change to make connection feel safer, easier or more meaningful?
Use about four minutes. You don’t need to cover all four questions. Keep identifying details private, and hold anything you don’t know as a question. You can reflect individually if you’re watching on your own. Pause the video for the discussion.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s come back to the last question: what could educators change around the student? If you’re together, you might offer one practical possibility without describing the student.
Notice whether your idea makes room for the kind of connection the student values. Does it change an expectation, an activity, a space or the pace of interaction? Does it leave room for choosing when to join and when to step back? The aim is meaningful connection for that person. We don’t need to make everyone look social in the same way.

segments.spoken_text:
Now we’ll look at daily capacity. Communication and connection are part of a much larger day, and that day asks different amounts of energy from different students.
As we move into the next activities, we’ll use a simple question: what costs, and what lightens? That language will help us look beyond a single task to the pattern of demands and opportunities for recovery across the day.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 14: Managing Daily Capacity. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 14; supplied slide, speaker notes and matching facilitator guide. Adapted/reused spoken delivery checked against this audience and the current Participant Guide. Primary source segment: s03_sl14_a. Session 3, active slide 14; slide text, speaker notes and corresponding facilitator guide.

segments.spoken_text:
Think of a student’s available energy as a battery. Each day starts with some charge, and it isn’t necessarily the same amount as yesterday. Activities and demands draw on that energy. As the battery runs lower, managing the next demand can become harder.
You may also hear people in the Autistic community talk about spoons. The idea is having a limited supply available: an action uses one spoon or several, and when spoons are low, there is less left for the next thing. These are ways of talking about capacity, rather than a measure we can calculate for someone else.
The other part of the picture is recharging. The right supports can reduce demand and help restore some capacity. A pause, useful information, a preferred way to communicate or a safe connection may make a difference, depending on the person.
So we’ll look for both sides in a school day: what draws on capacity, and what helps to restore it. What helps one student may be different for another.
segments.source_note: Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 15: Batteries and Spoons Think of a student's energy as a battery.. Supplied slide text, complete speaker notes, matching Facilitator Guide and current Participant Guide checked. Early Career Teachers Session 3, slide 15; supplied slide, speaker notes and matching facilitator guide. Adapted/reused spoken delivery checked against this audience and the current Participant Guide. Primary source segment: s03_sl15_a. Session 3, active slide 15; slide text, speaker notes and corresponding facilitator guide.

segments.spoken_text:
Capacity fluctuates. Like all of us, Autistic students can have easier days and harder days. Stress, energy, sensory demands and what else is happening in life can change what is manageable.
That means the same student may do something one day and need more support with it the next. Yesterday’s success doesn’t prove that today’s difficulty is a choice, and finishing a task doesn’t tell us how much effort it required.
Hold that in mind when you look at the students you know. We can ask what is different today, what demands have already accumulated, and what support is available now. We don’t have to know every cause before making information clearer or allowing a useful pause. We do need to keep checking with the student and the people who know them, instead of treating capacity as fixed.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to page thirteen. We’re going to map a typical day in your classroom from arrival to departure. If you don’t have your own class yet, use a placement class or a class you know well. In secondary, follow a student’s day across periods, rooms and teachers. Relief teachers can draw on a recent booking or a class they return to often.
Start with a simple timeline. Then add the routines, transitions and changes that matter in your setting.
Follow the students’ experience as well as the official timetable. Where are the shifts between tasks, the waiting, the movement and the breaks? Where can a student communicate, choose, pause or recover? Include sensory and communication demands where you know they are relevant.
Then mark how the same moments may land for each of the two or three students you have in mind. You can use different marks for different students, without names or identifying incidents. If you don’t know how a moment is experienced, leave it as a question.
Leave some room on your map: we’ll add another layer next. Allow about six minutes, with optional discussion with a partner. Keep the map private unless you choose to discuss it. Pause the video while you work.

Let’s pause our drawing there. You don’t need a polished or complete map. This is a working picture to extend, rather than a judgement of a student or a school.
Look briefly at the same point in the day for your different students. It may involve different communication, sensory or task demands for each of them. That is why we’re keeping several real students in view. Keep the map beside you; it will travel with us into Session Four.

segments.spoken_text:
Now turn to page fourteen and return to your day map. Use one mark or colour for what costs: what adds demand or uncertainty. Use another for what lightens: what reduces demand, restores capacity or brings joy. Think back to the battery image: what drains, and what might recharge?
Add questions where a student’s experience isn’t known. Something can be enjoyable or successfully completed and still take considerable effort. We can record what we observe, but we can’t read an internal state from a single moment.
Include strengths, joy, safe connection and belonging. We want a picture of what sustains a student as well as what is difficult. Give yourself about four minutes to add this layer, and pause the video while you do.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.

segments.spoken_text:
Come back to the pattern across the day. Where do several demands occur close together? Where are the opportunities for relief or recovery? What is already working well and worth protecting?
Treat these marks as prompts for inquiry, not a score. What costs or lightens can differ between students, and for the same student on different days. Choose one pattern you would like to understand better. Keep that question on your day map. We will use it in Session Four to consider what could be ready for students from day one.

segments.spoken_text:
This school-day stack gives us another way to see accumulation. The darker bars represent demand. The lighter bars represent relief and recovery. They’re a visual cue, rather than quantities we can assign to a child.
A moment that looks small by itself may arrive after many other demands. The last transition of the day sits within everything that came before it. Equally, a supportive interaction or an opportunity to recover belongs in the picture too.
So when we notice a difficult moment, we can ask what the day has already asked of this student and what support has been available. Keep this qualitative. We’re looking for patterns and questions that help us improve access, while keeping relief, recovery and joy visible alongside cost.

segments.spoken_text: There are other things that can draw on our batteries or spoons, including effort that isn’t obvious to someone watching. Let’s hear the next video about masking. Keep in mind the difference between how a person appears on the outside and what they may be managing.

segments.spoken_text: As we return from the video, keep that distinction open. Visible behaviour gives us part of the picture. We’ll now connect this with identity, capacity and belonging at school.

segments.spoken_text:
A student can appear fine without feeling fine. Quietness, compliance or completed work doesn’t give us a full account of what someone is managing. Masking brings that question into our thinking about identity and belonging.
Hold four questions in mind. What might this student be working hard to manage or hide? Where can they be recognised and included? What supports belonging without requiring them to appear less Autistic? And what does the student want others to understand?
We can’t answer those questions simply by watching from the outside. They invite us to listen and to examine the conditions around the student. Include what feels safe and joyful, the connections they value, and places where they can be themselves.
This is a reason to look beyond whether a task was finished or a lesson was quiet. Access matters, and so do the effort involved and the student’s experience of belonging.

segments.spoken_text:
Return to page twelve for the masking discussion. With a partner, consider three questions. When might one of the students you have in mind be working hard to appear fine at school when they are not? When and where do they seem most comfortable being themselves? What could we change to help them feel more comfortable and supported?
You have about three minutes. Keep examples anonymised and distinguish what you know from what you wonder. Avoid assuming that a quiet student is coping, or that outward behaviour tells you the whole story. Pause the video for the conversation.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s come back together. Focus on one possible change, rather than a conclusion about what a student must be feeling. If you’re sharing with colleagues, offer the change without identifying the child.
Perhaps your next step is to ask a better question, understand an existing source of comfort, or change a demand in a routine. Whatever you choose, keep the student’s perspective central. The aim is to make being themselves safer and better supported, and to find out whether the change helps.

segments.spoken_text:
You don’t need all the answers. You need a way to find out and adjust. Look back at your day map, especially the questions you wrote where a student’s experience was unknown. Those are useful starting points.
Keep what you have seen separate from what you think it means. You might know that a student left an activity, but still need to understand the information, demands or experience around that moment. A clear observation gives you something concrete to discuss with the student and the people who know them.
If a strategy isn’t working for a student, trying a different one is part of teaching. You can review what happened, ask for another perspective and adjust. Knowing who to ask is part of professional practice too. You are not expected to resolve every concern or make every decision alone.
A useful next step may be one observation, one question or one conversation. Let’s make that practical by looking at what it means to be new in a school.

Notice what you see, keep your questions open, and know who to ask. If a strategy isn't working for a student, try a different one. That is part of teaching, not a failure.. segments.spoken_text:
When you’re new, you are learning much more than a timetable. You’re learning the staffroom routines, who makes different decisions, where information lives and how this particular school works. That takes time.
You can learn those local ways while holding a neurodiversity-affirming approach. If you notice a practice that raises a question, begin with its purpose and what a student may experience. An experienced colleague may know its history, the reasons for it, or what has already been tried.
Keep the conversation about the practice and its effect on students. Bring a careful observation and an open question to your mentor, a team meeting or the relevant local process. You don’t have to resolve a school-wide practice by yourself. Start with what you can influence in your own room.
Look for colleagues who share this approach and can help you think. Asking questions early can help you find those people. For casual and relief teachers, that can mean learning the key contacts in several different schools, sometimes with very little time on site.
Think briefly about one thing you are still learning about how your school works. Who might help you understand it? Keep that question ready. The support map on the next slide is where you can record the people you need.

segments.spoken_text:
Open page fifteen, Your support map. Put yourself in the centre. Around you, name the real people you can go to at school, using roles or first names only. This is about your supports, so we don’t need to describe an incident or identify a student.
Start with two different situations. A student is distressed right now: who do you call or send for? A worry has been building over time: who do you talk to? Those may lead to different people and processes.
Then add who helps you think a situation through, someone who shares this approach, and the formal supports in your setting. That might include wellbeing staff, learning support, your mentor and leaders. Include the student and family as people who hold important knowledge.
If you work casually or across several schools, you can make one map per school, or start with the one you know best. If you haven’t started in a school yet, use a placement setting or list the roles you will look for when you begin.
Take five minutes on your own. Mark the gaps in the box at the bottom. Then spend about three minutes with a partner, comparing the kinds of support you have identified and choosing one idea for filling a gap. You can keep details private. Pause the video now for the mapping and conversation.

segments.spoken_text:
Let’s come back to the gaps. Choose one step you can take this term to fill one: a person to introduce yourself to, a role to locate, or a question to take to your mentor.
A blank on this page is something to find out. Schools organise their supports differently, so check how the roles and processes work in your setting. Keep the map alongside your day map. It will help with the asking list in the next session.
Don’t carry a worry about a student on your own. Knowing who can help, and how to reach them, is part of being prepared.

segments.spoken_text:
On page sixteen, let’s check the school pathway before it is needed. Work through the four questions here while things are calm.
Who do you contact in the moment, and afterwards? What process does your school follow for wellbeing and safety? What information will you bring? And who can help when the next step is unclear?
Aim for a clear, factual account: what you saw and heard, when it happened and what happened before. Keep an observation separate from a guess about what the student was feeling.
Circle any question you can’t answer yet and note who you will ask. Your mentor or a leader can help you locate the relevant procedure and understand your role. Procedures differ across schools and systems, so use the pathway for the setting you are in.
Take a moment to check your answers and mark what you need to find out. Pause the video if you need longer.

segments.spoken_text:
Keep those questions with your support map and find the answers before you need them. Clear information and known contacts make it easier to involve the right people.
We’ll close the morning by returning to the students you’ve been thinking about. After the next slide, take your lunch break. The live workshop allows twelve thirty to one. Bring your day map and support map back for Session Four.

segments.spoken_text:
Across Sessions Two and Three, you’ve been building a picture of those students. How the world arrives through their senses. How each thinks, focuses and builds understanding. Their strengths and interests. Their internal experience. How they reach towards other people, and what that can cost when the conditions don’t support them.
Managing a school day can involve sensory demands, social interpretation, executive effort and communication across differences. Sometimes it also involves working to appear fine when fine is not what is happening. That effort uses resources.
A child who knows who they are, and feels valued for it, has more of those resources available for learning, connection and self-knowledge. The research discussed in this workshop connects a positive sense of Autistic identity with better mental health and wellbeing. Belonging matters. So does agency: meaningful choice about how to communicate, where to be, and when to step back.
Knowing that other Autistic people share your experience can matter too. There are Autistic adults and communities in which people find belonging and purpose. These students are not alone.
This belongs within our educational work. We can make room for identity, connection and self-understanding in the conditions we create every day. Take that thought with you into the break.
The deepest thing you can do is support them to know themselves, and to know that who they are is worth knowing.
